justification: Deep, well-structured article that clears the bar against GeeksforGeeks's BFS-vs-DFS page (which is a comparison table with no complexity analysis, no iterative-DFS pitfall, and no C#-specific notes) and matches Sedgewick & Wayne's own algs4 site in rigor while adding a C# angle it doesn't have. run-code is green and deterministic: I ran it 4 times from this worktree and got byte-identical PASS (blocks=32 executed=16) every time, and .verify/code/algorithms__breadth-first-and-depth-first-search.json confirms every one of the 16 run blocks individually reports ok:true. I independently reproduced the article's central claim from scratch, with my own graph and variable names (A/B/C/D/E, not Config/Database/...): a recursive DFS with true onPath/done classification calls A->E and C->D 'nontree' (forward/cross) on an acyclic graph, while a naive iterative DFS that classifies purely on 'seen.Contains(next)' calls C->D 'back' -- a false cycle signal on a graph with no cycle. This matches the article's own demonstrated failure mode (Logging->Repository, Logging->Client, Cache->Service misclassified as 'back' in the modules graph) and confirms the claim generalizes, not just on the article's specific example. I re-derived every complexity claim (BFS/DFS/cycle-detection/toposort/components all O(V+E), adjacency-matrix traversal O(V^2), O(V) space) and they are correct and match the empirical edge-count table in 'What both cost'. I fetched and checked every cited source: Sedgewick & Wayne's 41graph and 42digraph pages support every attributed claim, and all five quoted fragments ('computes a shortest path from s to v'; 'explores the vertices adjacent to v in the reverse order of the standard recursive DFS'; 'may be updated more than once, so it may not be suitable for backtracking applications'; 'reverse postorder in a DAG provides a topological order'; 'time proportional to the sum of [the] degrees') are verbatim against the live pages, correctly attributed, and not closely paraphrased beyond the quoted fragment. CLRS is cited only by chapter name, never a page, which is the brief's required fallback for a textbook not opened online, and 'Elementary Graph Algorithms' is CLRS's actual, well-known chapter for exactly this content (BFS, DFS, back-edge cycle theorem, DFS-based topological sort). One real factual error, however: the :::dotnet callout claims 'Both [Queue<T> and Stack<T>] document O(1) for the operations a graph search calls in a loop -- Enqueue/Dequeue and Push/Pop -- except when a push forces a reallocation, which the docs call out as the one O(n) case for Stack<T>.Push.' I fetched Microsoft's own Queue<T>.Enqueue method page, and its Remarks say the identical thing about Enqueue: 'If Count is less than the capacity of the internal array, this method is an O(1) operation. If the internal array needs to be reallocated to accommodate the new element, this method becomes an O(n) operation.' So the O(n) reallocation case is not unique to Stack<T>.Push as the article states -- Queue<T>.Enqueue has the exact same documented exception. Worse, the article's link for the Queue<T> claim points at the class-overview page (system.collections.generic.queue-1), which I also fetched directly and which states no Big-O for Enqueue/Dequeue at all; the complexity language only exists on the method-specific pages, which are not linked. Per the rubric, a single factual error caps the technical score at 7, so the score reflects an otherwise ~9-level article capped there.

issues.location: The :::dotnet callout after the 'one-line swap' section, sentence beginning 'Both document O(1) for the operations a graph search calls in a loop'
issues.problem: Factually wrong and misattributed. Microsoft Learn's Queue<T>.Enqueue Remarks state the exact same O(n)-on-reallocation exception the article attributes only to Stack<T>.Push: 'If the internal array needs to be reallocated to accommodate the new element, this method becomes an O(n) operation, where n is Count.' The article's own claim that this is 'the one O(n) case for Stack<T>.Push' is therefore false -- Enqueue has an identical documented exception, and Dequeue/Pop are the ones with no exception. Compounding this, the Queue<T> link in the callout points at the class-overview page, which (verified by fetch) states no Big-O for Enqueue/Dequeue anywhere on it; the complexity language lives only on the Enqueue and Dequeue method pages, which are not linked.
issues.fixLooksLike: Rewrite to state the true, symmetric picture: Enqueue and Push are both O(1) unless the backing array needs to reallocate, in which case both become O(n); Dequeue and Pop are always O(1) (no reallocation on removal). Link Queue<T>.Enqueue and Queue<T>.Dequeue method pages (not just the class page) alongside Stack<T>.Push/Pop, since that is where the Big-O remarks actually live.
